markdown.markdown:
The Alzheimer's Biomarkers Consortium–Down Syndrome (ABC-DS) is a longitudinal
research study focused on understanding the development and progression of
Alzheimer's disease (AD) in adults with Down syndrome (DS). The study collects
clinical, cognitive, neuroimaging, biomarker, and other research data to
characterize changes associated with AD and identify factors that may influence
disease progression.

ABC-DS data are made available to approved researchers through the Laboratory of
Neuro Imaging (LONI) Image and Data Archive (IDA). Because the study includes
multiple types of data collected across research sites and repeated visits,
understanding how the data are organized is an important first step before
beginning an analysis.

This guide provides a practical introduction to accessing, navigating, and
working with the ABC-DS data. It is intended for researchers who are new to the
dataset, external to ABC-DS, or who need a reference for locating, interpreting,
and processing study files.

The guide covers the following topics:

- A background and history of ABC-DS.
- Study design and data collection procedures.
- Data organization, freezes, and upload dates.
- Understanding data dictionaries and codebooks.
- Navigating LONI and downloading data.

By the end of this guide, users should be better equipped to locate relevant
data, understand the contents of downloaded files, and identify the
documentation needed to prepare ABC-DS data for analysis.

## What is ABC-DS

ABC-DS is a multisite, longitudinal research study involving participants
recruited and assessed at research sites across the United States and the United
Kingdom. Data are collected through a coordinated study protocol that includes
clinical and cognitive assessments, neuroimaging, biological sample collection,
and other research measures.

The study is longitudinal, meaning participants return for repeated assessments
over time. Participants are invited to complete follow-up visits approximately
every 16 months, allowing researchers to examine changes in cognition, clinical
characteristics, biomarkers, and other outcomes as participants age.

Because data are collected across multiple sites and repeated visits, the
resulting dataset includes information from different participants, assessment
time points, and types of research procedures. Individual measures may be stored
in separate files, and not every participant will necessarily have data
available for every measure or visit.

When working with ABC-DS data, it is important to consider:

- **Demographic and clinical data:** Participant characteristics, medical
history, and clinical assessments.
- **Cognitive and functional assessments:** Measures of cognition and other
outcomes used to characterize changes in functioning.
- **Neuroimaging data:** Imaging acquisitions and derived measures used to
assess brain structure and pathology.
- **Biomarker data:** Measures from biological samples that may help
characterize Alzheimer's disease-related processes.
- **Additional research measures:** Other assessments or derived variables
collected as part of the study.

The availability of specific measures, variables, and files depends on the data
release and applicable access permissions. Researchers should consult the
documentation accompanying each release to determine which data are available
and how individual measures are defined.

## History of ABC-DS

ABC-DS began in 2015 as two coordinated research programs funded through
separate National Institutes of Health (NIH) awards:

- Neurodegeneration in Aging Down Syndrome (NiAD): NIH award U01AG051406.
- Alzheimer's Disease in Down Syndrome (ADDS): NIH award U01AG051412.

These programs brought together research teams investigating Alzheimer's disease
biomarkers and disease progression in adults with DS. Although funded
separately, the teams collaborated toward shared scientific goals.

In September 2020, the continuation of this work was funded through a single,
integrated consortium award, U19AG068054, supported by the National Institute on
Aging (NIA), the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and
Human Development (NICHD), and the NIH INCLUDE Project.

This integrated effort continued the collaborative, multisite longitudinal study
and expanded the availability of harmonized research data. Today, ABC-DS
provides a comprehensive resource for investigating clinical, cognitive,
neuroimaging, and biomarker changes associated with Alzheimer's disease in
adults with DS.
